回复 @mitchellh
libghostty-vt 1.0.2 released: correct widths for skin tone emoji, insert/delete line (IL/DL) fixes, up to 1.8x faster scrolling inside left/right margins (think tmux side-by-side panes or Neovim vertical splits), and more. Release notes below.

https://lib.ghostty.org/vt/release-notes.html

Bug Fixes:

- The mouse encoder no longer forgets the last cell when calling `ghostty_mouse_encoder_set_from_terminal` and setting the size now only forget it when the value actually changes. Previously, with `GHOSTTY_MOUSE_ENCODER_OPT_TRACK_LAST_CELL` on, motion in the same cell was reported again, so a click could come out as a press, a motion and a release. This isn't incorrect VT sequencing, but it was wasteful and unnecessary.
- With grapheme clustering (mode 2027), a skin tone modifier now makes an emoji that is text by default 2 cells wide, the same as VS16. For example, U+261D U+1F3FB (index pointing up, light skin tone) was 1 cell and is now 2. `ghostty_unicode_grapheme_width` changes the same way.
- Terminals created with the C API now ignore the Kitty drag and drop protocol (OSC 72), including its queries. The C API can't deliver drops yet, so programs registered for drops that never came instead of falling back.
- Insert and delete lines (IL and DL) no longer break the soft wraps of rows that move together. Previously a wrapped line in the scroll region, such as a long URL, became two lines until the program redrew it.
- Insert and delete lines with left and right margins no longer drop the semantic prompt marks (OSC 133) of the rows they move, so scrolling by prompts no longer skips prompts.
- Kitty graphics: Unicode placeholders no longer disappear when insert or delete lines with left and right margins move their row.
- A restored snapshot now keeps a pending wrap at any column, for both the cursor and the saved cursor (DECSC). Previously it was kept only on the last column, so with a right margin (DECSLRM) the next character overwrote the cursor cell instead of wrapping. The snapshot format is unchanged.

Performance:

- Insert and delete lines with left and right margins now move styled rows with a single copy. This is how tmux scrolls a pane next to another pane, and how Neovim scrolls a vertical split. A stream that does this went from 1,716 to 936 ms on x86_64 (1.8x) and from 1,100 to 695 ms on an M1 Pro (1.6x).
- Hyperlinks (OSC 8) are hashed in one pass instead of a byte at a time. `ls -laR --hyperlink=always` output is 1.3x faster.
- Carriage returns and absolute column moves (CHA, HPA) no longer look up the cursor's row again. Scrolling streams are up to 6% faster.
- Erasing cells skips rows that are already blank and releases styles a run at a time instead of a cell at a time. Erase-heavy streams are 3–6% faster.

NAND spot prices are falling.
Consumer SSD prices may follow with a lag.

The 512Gb TLC wafer spot sat around $14.2 mid-month. That is down about 20% from mid-to-late October and about 32% from the August high of $21. Consumer SSD prices have not moved much yet. They are expected to drop later.

Demand has weakened. Higher memory prices lifted PC and smartphone costs. Buyers are delaying purchases. Phone and PC makers are cutting base storage to hold costs. Consumer NAND demand came in weaker than expected.

Supply is rising. Samsung and SK Hynix are prioritizing high-margin enterprise SSD, DRAM and HBM. YMTC, now the third-largest, is stronger in consumer NAND. It finished a third fab at about 100,000 wafers a month and will make both NAND and new DRAM there. It already covers a large share of Chinese NAND demand and sells consumer SSDs under the ZHITAI brand at lower prices than similar Samsung models.

YMTC wafer capacity is projected to rise from 2.01 million this year to 2.5 million next year, up 24.2%. Other makers’ new fabs come later. YMTC can gain share and press consumer prices. Other suppliers are also raising layer counts and QLC mix before new capacity arrives.

TrendForce sees 2027 NAND bit supply up 25-30%. Bank of America expects consumer NAND contract prices to fall another 5-10% in the first quarter of next year.

Enterprise SSD demand remains the key variable. If AI investment slows after the midterms and data-center builds slip, volume could shift toward consumer and add more price pressure. The reverse is also possible. Consumer NAND is still expected to ease into next year, but a return to pre-2025 SSD prices looks unlikely with the new data-center demand.

Thanks for the question. The 30% number doesn't line up with what NVIDIA reports.

The Singapore figure people point to was a billing number, not a shipping number. Under the old reporting, Singapore was about 18% of fiscal 2025 revenue and 21-22% in the first half of fiscal 2026. But NVIDIA said shipments to Singapore were under 2% of revenue, and that over 99% of the controlled data center compute billed there was for US-based customers. It was mostly where large US customers send their invoices.

Late last year NVIDIA switched to reporting revenue by where the customer is headquartered and recast prior years. On that basis China, including Hong Kong, peaked at about 19% of revenue in fiscal 2025, was about 9% for fiscal 2026, and about 8% in the July quarter. Licensed Hopper sales to China in the October quarter were $2.4 billion, about 2% of revenue, and they are already out of the guide.

Why we don't see it as the main issue: NVIDIA is still supply constrained, so parts that can't go to China get sold to someone else, and management raised next year's growth outlook to about 75% after the new export rules came out.

The part of the bear case we take seriously is the offshore angle. If Chinese demand was being served through Southeast Asian neoclouds and the new rules shut that off, that capacity comes back to market. In a tight year it gets absorbed. It shows up when supply loosens, which is 2028, and that is the same window where we already moved our view toward risk.
